hints: Start by recalling what a gene mutation actually changes - the sequence of bases in DNA that will be transcribed into mRNA.
Compare swapping one base for another with adding or removing one or two bases - think about how the mRNA codons will be read differently.
Remember the genetic code is degenerate, so think about when changing one base might leave the amino acid unchanged.
Think about what happens to every codon downstream if you insert or delete a number of bases that is not a multiple of three.
Link any change in codons to the sequence of amino acids joined together during translation.
Consider how a different amino acid sequence changes bonding and folding, so the final 3D shape of the protein changes.
Think about a special codon change that can stop translation early and give a short non-functional polypeptide or enzyme.
For Huntington's, recall whether the mutant allele is dominant or recessive and what that means for a heterozygote.
Think about which organ is affected, what symptoms this causes, and why symptoms only show in middle age despite being present from birth.
walkthrough:
Sort Out The Two Main Types Of Gene Mutation**
Think of DNA as a sentence read in three-letter words called codons. A substitution just swaps one letter for another, so only one codon changes. An insertion or deletion adds or removes letters, so if the number is not three, every word after that point is misread. That misreading is called a frameshift.

Why Substitution Is Often Harmless But Frameshift Is Serious**
Because the code is degenerate, several codons code for the same amino acid. So a substitution may still give the same amino acid and is called silent, with no change in phenotype. A frameshift changes many amino acids at once, so the phenotype is almost always strongly altered. A common student mistake is to say all mutations cause disease - most substitutions do nothing.

From DNA Change To Broken Protein**
The changed codons change the primary structure, which is the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide made at translation. Different amino acids have different R groups, so hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds form in different places. That changes folding into the tertiary 3D shape. If the active site of an enzyme or functional region is distorted, you get loss of function. If the mutation creates a premature stop codon, translation stops early and you get a short useless protein.

Apply This To Huntington's Disease**
Huntington's is caused by a dominant mutant allele, so only one copy is needed and heterozygotes will show the disease. The mutation is an expansion of the CAG base triplet repeat, giving many more repeats than normal. More repeats tend to give earlier onset and greater severity.

Link To Phenotype And Timing**
The faulty protein causes brain cells to die more rapidly than normal, so the brain degenerates. That leads to involuntary movements, mental deterioration such as memory and reasoning loss, and mood changes. Onset is typically in middle age, so there is no change in phenotype in earlier life, which is why the allele can be passed on before diagnosis.

Final answer: Substitution of a base often has no significant effect as it is a silent mutation due to the degenerate code. Insertion or deletion of bases causes a frameshift, altering all downstream codons, so has a significant phenotypic effect. Amino acid sequence / primary structure changes, altering tertiary structure / 3D folding, causing loss of protein / enzyme function, e.g. premature stop codon gives shortened polypeptide. Huntington's mutant allele is dominant due to expanded CAG triplet repeats, so heterozygotes develop disease. Causes rapid brain cell death / brain degeneration leading to involuntary movements, mental deterioration and mood changes, with onset in middle age and earlier / more severe onset with more repeats.

Think about the first step in any hormone response - binding to a receptor protein.

walkthrough:
Set The Scene In The Aleurone Layer**
In a germinating barley or cereal seed, the embryo releases gibberellin which acts on the aleurone layer surrounding the starch-filled endosperm. Those aleurone cells need to make amylase to digest starch to maltose for the embryo. Without gibberellin, that gene is switched off.

How The Gene Is Kept Off By DELLA**
The off switch is a group of repressor proteins called DELLA proteins. They bind to and inhibit a transcription factor called PIF, so PIF cannot work. No transcription factor means no transcription of the amylase gene.

How Gibberellin Removes The Block**
Gibberellin binds to its receptor in the aleurone cells. That complex activates an enzyme system that targets DELLA proteins for breakdown. This is not just reversible inhibition, the DELLA protein is destroyed, so the block is fully removed.

Switching On Amylase Production**
With DELLA gone, free PIF binds to the promoter region of the DNA for the amylase gene. That stimulates transcription to make mRNA coding for amylase, which is then translated on ribosomes to produce amylase protein for secretion into the endosperm.

Final answer: In the aleurone layer DELLA proteins inhibit transcription factor PIF. Gibberellin binds to its receptor, activating an enzyme that breaks down DELLA proteins. Freed PIF / TF binds to the promoter region of the amylase gene, stimulating transcription of mRNA coding for amylase, followed by translation into amylase.
